analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal board to cap excessive prices on prescription drugs and medical devices.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2018, referred to three House committees and a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a review board inside HHS that collects price and cost data from every drug and device maker, defines what counts as an 'excessive' price, and bans charging one. A manufacturer caught overcharging could face fines of up to 10% of the product's sales, a shorter patent, higher Medicaid rebates to states, and a special tax on the overcharge. Anyone could petition the board to review a price, and individuals could import comparable drugs from approved countries when a US maker was overcharging. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take prescription drugs or use medical devices — essentially everyone — would benefit if price-gouging were capped and cheaper imported alternatives became legally available. Medicaid programs in the states would gain from higher rebates, and federal agencies that buy drugs would get recommendations to switch to cheaper products.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to disclose prices and production costs and bans charging an 'excessive price' for any prescription drug or medical device, with the board judging prices against comparable drugs, foreign prices, production costs, and inflation.

Enforces the cap through penalties: civil fines of up to 10% of gross sales of the product, shortened patents of up to 5 years, higher Medicaid rebates paid to states, and a tax on the gap between the charged price and the reasonable price.
Lets any person petition the board to review a drug's price, and allows individuals to safely import comparable drugs from approved countries when a US manufacturer is charging an excessive price.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug and medical device manufacturers would bear the cost: price caps, fines of up to 10% of sales of an overpriced product, shortened patent terms, higher Medicaid rebates, and a tax on excessive prices. Shareholders in those firms would absorb lower profits.

drawbacks.text: Price controls set by formula can discourage investment in new medicines; the bill would penalize prices above a government-determined 'reasonable price', which manufacturers argued (in general debates over similar proposals) could slow drug development.

The board's power to shorten patent terms and impose a tax on the gap between the charged price and a government-determined price would put pricing decisions in the hands of a federal board, a significant expansion of government control over a major industry that courts and future Congresses might have to unwind.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large — an enforceable cap on excessive drug and device prices, with penalties, a public petition process, and a legal route to cheaper imports. The drawbacks are real: price controls set by formula can be crude, could deter investment in some new medicines or devices, and the board's reach into patent terms and pricing raises practical and legal questions no committee ever examined. On balance the bill would have shifted bargaining power from manufacturers to patients and public programs, but it got no hearing, so those tradeoffs were never tested in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then a subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on May 9, 2018, joined by two cosponsors, Representatives Lloyd Doggett and Gwen Moore, both Democrats.

The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on May 25, 2018, and no further action was taken.
No committee reported the bill, no vote occurred in either chamber, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug and medical device manufacturers are better off: their pricing was never capped and no penalties, rebates, or importation rights took effect.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prescription Drug and Medical Device Price Review Board Act of 2018 on May 9, 2018.

for.name: Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Gwen Moore

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees (115th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee, held no hearings, and never scheduled it for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported it, but no vote was ever taken so party positions on the merits were never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would cap what they can charge, exposing violators to fines up to 10% of sales, shortened patents, higher Medicaid rebates, and a tax on excessive prices. Patients and federal health programs would pay less; manufacturers' pricing freedom would end.
Devices sold in the US would be subject to the same excessive-price prohibition and penalties as drugs, a sector that largely escapes federal price regulation today.
